Zero, First, Second, and Third Conditional Review
Conditionals refer to any sentence with an if clause and a result clause.

We use the zero conditional to convey logical conclusions. It is formed by the present simple in the –if clause and in the –result clause.
Example:

If some software developments can do harm, others can do well in the society.

We use the first conditional to talk about the future. If the condition is met then the statement is likely to happen. It is formed by the present simple in the if clause, although the present continuous is also possible. The result clause is in the future tense. It can have many forms apart from the usual will; going to and present continuous with future meaning are used as well.

Example:

If they create a software capable of translating any language, no one will hire a translator anymore.

We use the second conditional to talk about imaginary or hypothetical situations. It is also called the unreal conditional. The verb in the -if clause is in the past simple and the verb in the result clause is preceded by the modal verb would, could or might.

Example:

If scientists developed an app to check your heart rate, many people would benefit from it.

The third conditional is used to talk about unreal situations in the past. This situation didn't happen but we're imagining the results. It is formed by the past perfect in the if clause, and the -result clause uses would have and the past participle of the verb.

Example:

If scientists had studied the impact of CO2 that cars produced, engineers would have created eco-friendly cars by now.
If I were able to change one thing in our day to day lives, I would choose traffic jams.
If we had realized sooner that cars pollute so much, we could have developed eco-friendly vehicles sooner.
If the same software is capable of such harm, it can help in numerous ways too.
Past Modals Review
We use past modals when we want to express past possibilities or imaginary situations that didn’t end up as expected.

The most commonly used modals in the past are should, could, and would; to use these modal verbs in the past you must follow this structure:

 

Subject+ modal verb + have + main verb in past participle + complement

 

Remember that we use the present perfect with have after the modal verb to refer to past expectations.

 

Should have:

Should is the modal verb we use for giving advice, so use should have when you want to mention the best way things should have been done. 

Examples:

You should have used the GPS system to find your way.

We should have bought an eco-friendly car.

 

Could have:

Use could have to talk about possibilities in the unreal past; if you want to underline other suitable options if past was different.

Examples:

I could have finished my work earlier, but I have a slow internet connection.

We could have done that faster with this new app.

 

Would have:

When you want to express imagined final results in the past, use the modal verb would have; remember that would have expresses more certainty than could have. 

Examples:

The manager would have saved lots of money with that new software.

You would have done that better with a better engine.
If we had realized sooner that cars pollute so much, we could have developed eco-friendly vehicles sooner.
I think that scientists and engineers from decades ago could have never imagined such developments.
Some people argue that software engineering should have never been created.

Punctuation and Capitalization
We use different kinds of punctuation marks in a text to provide cohesion and coherent. On the other hand, capitalization helps us to understand some important words.

The two more used punctuation marks are the comma and the period.

We use the period at the end of a sentence. When there is a question or exclamation mark at the end of a sentence, the period is not used. The same happens when there is an abbreviation. The period used at the end of the abbreviation also serves as the period for the sentence.

Commas are very important punctuation marks as their absence can change the meaning of a sentence. You use the comma in the following cases:

  • To list different objects in a sequence. Do not place the comma after the last item of the list.
  • If a noun is being modified by a series of adjectives, they should be separated by commas.
  • When there is a dependent and independent clause in a sentence, we use the comma to separate them.

Regarding capitalization, remember that proper names and languages always have capital letters. On the other hand, the first word at the beginning of a sentence, or after a period is capitalized. Also, abbreviations are completely written in capital letters.

Examples:

General Motors

images.text: How will traffic and transportation be in the future? If I were able to change one thing in our day to day lives, I would choose traffic jams. IBM is about to launch a system to predict traffic jams before they occur. It uses GPS, roadside sensors, and archived data to predict congestion. The technology has been proven successful in trials. If we had realized sooner that cars pollute so much, we could have developed eco-friendly vehicles sooner. However, in the last years, cars have become cleaner, safer, and more affordable, but there is a long way to go. In 2015, Larry Burns, the VP of General Motors predicted that computer-enhanced vehicles that run on hydrogen are possible, and they could even channel energy back into the electrical grid when not in use.

The previous statements are examples of software engineering, a new science that many human lives depend on. In the past few years, newspaper's front pages have been swamped with headlines about the lack of privacy and security of software. It is true that software engineering has created some of the biggest concerns related to credit card theft, identity fraud, and technical malfunctions in cars and airplanes. Due to this, some people argue that software engineering should have never been created. Nevertheless, if the same software is capable of such harm, it can help in numerous ways too. It has already helped to prevent car collisions and improved the way doctors perform surgeries, among other advances.

Let's take a look at apps now; they are invaluable parts of our smartphones. If someone told you that apps would be so far-reaching that they would be able to conduct medical checkups or identify people through face-recognition, would you believe it? Apple and Google are creating face recognition software for cellphones. I think that scientists and engineers from decades ago could have never imagined such developments. Nowadays, they are trying their best to develop apps to measure blood pressure and heart rates. If they manage to create such powerful smartphones, I will definitely buy one!
